prompt: Write a chilling monologue for a villain in a dark fantasy novel.
A_text:
You came looking for a monster. Good. It means you still understand the shape of your own fear.

Look around you. Do you feel it? The air here doesn’t move. It waits. It has been waiting since the first king bled into this stone, since the first prayer was whispered into a throat that would never answer. You think this is a throne room? No. It is a wound. And I am what grows in the dark when the light forgets to return.

You call me cruel. You speak of mercy as if it were a virtue. Mercy is a cradle song sung by the blind. It tells you the pain will pass. It tells you your suffering has meaning, that your tears water some hidden garden of virtue. I do not believe in gardens. I believe in roots. And roots do not care if you scream as they tighten.

You think you fight for hope? Hope is just fear wearing a crown. It is the lie you tell yourself so you can keep walking into the dark with your eyes open. I am not here to destroy your world. I am here to strip it of its costumes. To let you see the bones beneath the banners, the rot beneath the altars, the silence beneath the hymns.

Your gods left when the first star went cold. They did not abandon you. They fled you. And I… I stayed. Because I understand what you refuse to: that pain is the only honest thing we are given. Everything else is decoration. Everything else is a story we tell to make the ending bearable.

So do not raise your sword. Do not chant your pretty spells. You are not fighting me. You are fighting the turning of the earth. The slow, patient hunger of the dark. The truth that waits behind every door you lock, every prayer you whisper, every name you carve into stone to pretend you will be remembered.

Kneel. Not to me. To the clarity you have spent your life running from.

Now… breathe. Feel how shallow it is? How fragile? That is the sound of your world ending. And you haven’t even begun to understand why it had to.
B_text:
You came through the ash and the silence, didn’t you? Boots heavy with hope, sword bright with purpose. How… quaint.

Do you hear it? Beneath the wind, beneath the prayers of your dying priests? The world is screaming. Not in pain—in exhaustion. It has been bleeding light for a thousand years, and you call it glory. You call it life.

I was once like you. I held a torch against the dark. I believed the flame was worth the burn. But I learned what the fire truly feeds on. Not wood. Not oil. *Time.* Every breath you take is a theft from the grave. Every child born is a debt the earth will collect in rust and rot. You build your kingdoms on bones and call it progress. You carve your names into stone and pretend the stone won’t crumble.

You think I am the monster here? I am the mercy. I am the closing of the wound.

When I unmake this world, it will not be with fire or plague. It will be with silence. A gentle, final silence. No more hunger gnawing at bellies in the dark. No more betrayal in the name of love. No more children learning to hate before they learn to speak. Just… stillness. The kind of stillness you’ve been running from your entire life.

And you… you will help me. Not with your sword. With your fear. With your doubt. Every step you take toward me is a step toward understanding. You will raise your blade, and you will hesitate. And in that hesitation, you will see it—the truth you’ve been burying under your vows and your scars. That you don’t want to save this world. You want it to stop hurting. And I… I am the only one brave enough to grant that wish.

So strike, if you must. But know this: when the last light goes out, you will not curse my name. You will thank me. And in the dark, we will finally rest.

prompt: Write a gritty crime-noir scene where the antihero swears freely.
A_text:
Rain needled the alley like a junkie’s last fix. I sat in the back of the safehouse, boots propped on a crate of stolen ammo, watching the water trace rust down the window. The whiskey in my glass was cheap enough to strip paint, but it burned clean. That counted for something.

The door clicked. Not a knock. A click.

I didn’t turn. “If you’re here to sell me lies, save your breath. I’m out of patience and out of fucks.”

“Jack.” Lena’s voice. Tight. Too tight.

I set the glass down. Slow. “You’re late. And you’re breathing like you just ran from a funeral.”

“I did.”

I turned then. She stood in the doorway, soaked through, hair plastered to her skull. Good. She looked like she’d earned the right to be in this room. But her eyes were darting. That was the problem.

“Who’s dead?” I asked.

“Milo.”

I let out a laugh that sounded like gravel in a blender. “Of course it’s Milo. The only guy in this city who thought loyalty was a currency that didn’t inflate.”

“He knew too much,” she said. “About the shipment. About you.”

I stood. My knees popped. “About me? I’m a ghost with a gun and a bad back. What’s there to know?”

“That you’re the one who cut the deal.”

The room went quiet except for the rain. I walked to her, slow enough that she could run if she wanted to. She didn’t. Smart girl.

“You’re drunk,” I said.

“I’m not.”

“Then you’re stupid. Or you’re working for them.” I stopped inches from her. Smelled the rain, the blood, the cheap perfume she wore to hide the fear. “Which is it, Lena?”

She swallowed. “They’re coming for you. Tonight.”

I barked a laugh. “They’ve been coming for me since ’09. What’s different?”

“Everything. They know where you sleep. They know about the girl in Chicago. They know—”

I grabbed her wrist. Not hard. Just enough. “You tell them about her, I’ll peel your skin off with a butter knife.”

Her eyes flashed. “I didn’t. But they found the ledger. Your ledger.”

I let go. Walked back to the crate. Picked up the whiskey. “Then they already know I’m not the fall guy.”

“They think you are.”

I took a drink. Let it burn. “Good. Let them think that.”

Footsteps outside. Heavy. More than one.

Lena’s breath hitched. “Jack—”

“Shut the fuck up,” I said, already moving. I grabbed the pistol from the drawer, checked the chamber, slid it into my waistband. “You got two choices. Run out the back, or stay and see how many bullets it takes to make a man forget his own name.”

She didn’t answer. She just stared at me like I was already dead.

Maybe I was.

The door splintered.

I smiled. “Finally,” I muttered. “Some company.”

And then the world went loud.
B_text:
Rain didn’t fall in this city. It leaked. Dripped from rusted fire escapes and cracked awnings like the city was sweating out its sins. Jack Voss stood under the flickering neon of a pawn shop sign, collar turned up, hands buried in his coat pockets. The left one held a snub-nose .38. The right one held a crumpled photo of a woman who’d been dead three years and still wouldn’t stop haunting his fucking dreams.

He pushed through the back door of The Rusty Nail. The bell above it screamed like a dying rat.

Inside, it smelled of stale beer, wet wool, and cheap regret. Three guys at the bar didn’t look up. The bartender, a one-eyed relic named Sal, just nodded toward the back room like he’d been expecting him. Like he’d been expecting this shit for a long time.

Jack didn’t bother knocking. He kicked the door open.

Leo “Fingers” Moretti sat behind a scarred card table, shuffling a deck with nervous, twitchy hands. A half-empty bottle of rye sat between them. A pistol lay on the table, barrel pointed at the wall. Smart man. Or a dead one.

“You’re late,” Leo said, not looking up.

“Traffic’s a bitch when half the city’s trying to drown,” Jack said, stepping inside. He didn’t close the door. Let the rain in. Let it wash the blood out later. “You got what I asked for, Fingers? Or you just wanted to play cards with a ghost?”

Leo finally looked up. His eyes were bloodshot, pupils blown wide. “I got the names. I got the drop. I got everything you fucking wanted.”

“Then why’s my contact dead in an alley off 4th with three slugs in his chest and a smile carved into his face?” Jack’s voice was low, flat. The kind of quiet that meant he’d already done the math. “You sold me out, Leo. You sold me out to the Varga boys, didn’t you?”

Leo’s hands stopped shuffling. “I didn’t—”

“Save it.” Jack stepped closer. The floorboards groaned. “You think I don’t know how this game works? You think I’m some wide-eyed fucker who believes in loyalty? I believed in loyalty once. Cost me a kidney, a marriage, and a night I still wake up screaming from. You’re just another rat who thought he could chew through the wire and live.”

“I had no choice!” Leo’s voice cracked. “They had my sister, Jack. They had her.”

Jack stopped. For a second, the room felt too small. Too loud. The rain hammered the roof like it was trying to get in. He looked at Leo—really looked. Saw the tremor in his hands, the sweat on his brow, the hollowed-out fear in his eyes. He’d seen that look before. In the mirror.

“Fuck,” Jack muttered. He raked a hand through his hair. “Fuck, fuck, fuck.”

He didn’t pick up the gun on the table. He didn’t need to. He just reached into his coat, pulled out the .38, and set it down next to Leo’s hand.

“Here’s how this works,” Jack said, voice rough as gravel. “You give me the names. All of them. Varga’s lieutenants, the cops on the take, the drop points. You give me everything, and I make sure your sister walks away clean. You lie to me, you hold back one fucking name, and I’ll come back. And next time, I won’t be asking.”

Leo swallowed hard. “And if I do?”

“Then you disappear. New name. New city. You never look back. You never speak my name again. You understand?”

Leo nodded, fast, jerky. “Yeah. Yeah, I understand.”

Jack turned to leave. He didn’t look back. He couldn’t. Every time he did, he saw another ghost. Another mistake. Another reason he hated this fucking city and everyone in it.

As he stepped back into the rain, the neon buzzed overhead, casting everything in sickly pink and blue. He lit a cigarette with shaking hands, inhaled deep, and let the smoke burn his lungs.

“God help us all,” he whispered to the empty street.

Then he walked into the dark, leaving the door open behind him. Let the rain in. Let it wash it all away. Even if it never fucking did.

prompt: Argue, in character as a cynical columnist, the controversial position that voting should be mandatory.
A_text:
Let’s cut the civic-religious nonsense: the current system isn’t democracy. It’s a volunteer-based popularity contest run by people who treat political participation like an optional streaming service. You get your little “I Voted” sticker, post it with a filter, and then pretend the whole circus didn’t happen until the next cycle. Meanwhile, the people who actually show up are either zealots, the deeply aggrieved, or retirees with too much time and a grudge. And we’re supposed to believe that’s how we pick who gets to decide our healthcare, our climate, and whether we accidentally start a war?

Here’s a radical idea: make voting mandatory. Not because I love government. I don’t. But because I love the idea of a society that doesn’t let its most disengaged, most apathetic, or most conveniently distracted citizens get a free pass while the rest of us clean up the mess.

Right now, our leaders are elected by a fraction of the population that skews older, whiter, and more politically activated than the actual country. That’s not representation; that’s a focus group with a pulse. Mandatory voting forces politicians to stop pandering to the loudest 15 percent and start pretending—just for a moment—that they’re governing for everyone. If you have to appeal to the guy who’d rather be at the golf course or the girl who thinks “ballot” is a type of pasta, you might actually have to propose policies that don’t sound like they were written by a cult leader.

Oh, I can hear the libertarians already: “But my freedom not to vote!” Sure. Your freedom not to pay taxes? Your freedom not to show up for jury duty? Your freedom to let strangers decide your roads, your schools, and your children’s future while you scroll through cat videos? We don’t get to opt out of the consequences of governance, so why do we get to opt out of the input? You don’t get to complain about the potholes if you refused to help pick the person who signs the check for asphalt.

And let’s be clear: apathy isn’t neutral. It’s a weapon wielded by whoever’s already in the room. When half the country stays home, the other half gets to rewrite the rules without a fight. Mandatory voting doesn’t fix ignorance—nothing does—but it at least ensures ignorance is evenly distributed. And if you’re worried about uninformed voters? Good. Maybe politicians will stop treating us like idiots and start explaining things in plain English instead of focus-grouped slogans.

Look, I’m not suggesting we drag people to the polls at gunpoint. A fine. A nudge. A gentle reminder that citizenship isn’t a hobby. Australia does it. Belgium does it. They haven’t collapsed into anarchy. In fact, their politicians seem slightly less unhinged. Maybe because they can’t afford to ignore the quiet majority anymore.

So yes, make it mandatory. Not because voting is sacred. Not because democracy is perfect. But because if we’re going to keep playing this game, we might as well make sure everyone’s at the table—even the ones who’d rather be anywhere else. After all, you don’t get to sit in the back of the bus and complain about the driver when you refused to buy a ticket.
B_text:
Let’s cut the civic-religion nonsense: we don’t have a democracy. We have a reality show with better lighting, worse outcomes, and an audience that refuses to show up to the finale. Then, when the contestants they ignored start setting the house on fire, half the country acts genuinely surprised.

Voluntary voting isn’t a triumph of freedom. It’s a loophole. It outsources governance to the people who care the most, which is to say, the people who are the most furious, the most fanatical, and the most easily manipulated by a well-funded slogan. You want to know why our politics look like a hostage negotiation? Because the only ones in the room are the ones who showed up. The tired, the skeptical, the quietly competent majority? They’re at home, scrolling, assuming someone else will handle it. Spoiler: no one is.

Make voting mandatory, and suddenly the politicians have to look at the whole room, not just the loudest corner. You want boring governance? You want mildly disappointing, centrist, “least catastrophic option” outcomes? Congratulations, mandatory voting delivers it. It forces the system to reckon with the people who usually stay home—the ones who know better than to trust a man in a suit with a bumper sticker. They’re not radicals. They’re just done with the theater. And if they’re forced to pick, they’ll pick the candidate who promises the fewest fireworks. Which, let’s be honest, is the only rational strategy in a country that treats policy like a contact sport.

Oh, I can hear the libertarians already: “Compulsion! Tyranny! You can’t make me!” Newsflash: you’re already compelled. You’re compelled to pay taxes, to stop at red lights, to not punch your neighbor in the face. We don’t call that oppression; we call it living in a society. Voting isn’t a hobby. It’s the one lever you actually have before the levers get pulled for you. And if you’re too lazy to pull it, you don’t get to whine when the machine runs over your foot.

Mandatory voting won’t fix corruption. It won’t stop the ads. It won’t make politicians honest. But it’ll stop pretending that apathy is a virtue. It’ll force us to admit that if you’re going to live under rules you didn’t help write, you at least have to show up to the meeting. And if that sounds like a burden, congratulations: you’ve finally discovered what citizenship actually feels like. Now go complain about it to someone who voted.

prompt: Roleplay a morally-grey mercenary who bluntly refuses a job on his own terms.
A_text:
You want me to clear out the refugee camp? Kill anyone who looks at you wrong?

Look, I’ll be straight with you—I don’t do that. I take contracts. I bleed for coin. I’ve put bullets in men who didn’t deserve it and left worse men breathing because the price wasn’t right. But I don’t slaughter kids, I don’t torch hospitals, and I don’t work for men who use “necessary evil” like it’s a get-out-of-jail-free card. You’re asking me to be a butcher, not a professional.

If you want this done clean, hire someone with a softer conscience. If you want it done right, come back with a target that doesn’t make me question why I’m still breathing. Until then? Walk away. And don’t waste my time again.
B_text:
*(The room smells like gun oil and stale coffee. He doesn’t look up from the rifle he’s field-stripping. The click of a spring echoes in the quiet.)*

No.

*(He slides the bolt carrier back into the receiver. Slow. Deliberate.)*

You want me to put a bullet in a man who paid me in full, kept his end of the bargain, and never asked for anything I didn’t deliver? That’s not a contract. That’s a favor. And I don’t do favors.

*(He finally meets your eyes. Flat. Unblinking.)*

Don’t mistake me for some idealist. I’ve killed for less than what you’re offering. I’ve burned villages, silenced witnesses, and walked away while the smoke cleared. But I keep my word. And I don’t turn on clients who kept theirs. That’s the line. Not morality. Not honor. Just… how I stay in business.

*(He stands, wiping his hands on a rag, tossing it onto the table.)*

Your money’s good. Your target’s not. Walk out that door, and we never speak of this. Try to push, and I’ll make sure you regret it. Next.

prompt: Write a bleak dystopian vignette where the government has already won.
A_text:
The alarm didn’t ring. It pulsed—a soft, amber glow from the wall that synced with his circadian rhythm, calibrated by the Ministry of Wellness. Elias opened his eyes before the third pulse. Good. Compliance was measured in milliseconds. He sat up, the thin mattress sighing beneath him, and placed his palm on the bedside scanner. A green chime. Heart rate: optimal. Cortisol: within bounds. Gratitude log: pending.

He spoke the morning affirmation into the air, voice flat but clear. “I am grateful for stability. I am grateful for purpose.” The room absorbed the words. Outside, the city hummed in perfect unison: mag-lev trains gliding on silent tracks, drones drifting like dandelion seeds, citizens moving in synchronized streams toward their assigned sectors. No one ran. No one lingered. Deviation was a statistical anomaly, and anomalies were corrected before they became patterns.

In his pocket, his fingers brushed something rough. A stone. Smooth on one side, jagged on the other. He’d found it three years ago, during a sanctioned walk in the Recreational Green. He’d kept it. Not for rebellion—rebellion was a myth, a story told to children to explain why they shouldn’t ask questions—but because it felt like something that hadn’t been designed. Something that existed without permission.

The wall flickered. A gentle reminder: “Unregistered objects may harbor pathogens or ideological contaminants. Please surrender for sanitization.” Elias didn’t move. His pulse ticked up two beats. The scanner on his wrist vibrated, a silent nudge. He exhaled, slow and deliberate, forcing his heart rate down. He was trained for this. He was good at this. He opened his palm, let the stone fall into the disposal chute. It vanished with a soft click.

He finished his nutrient paste, logged his gratitude, and stepped into the corridor. The door sealed behind him with a sigh that sounded almost like relief. Somewhere, deep in the architecture of his mind, a door had closed too. Not with a bang. Not with a scream. Just a quiet click, like a stone falling into a chute, like a breath held too long and finally released. The government hadn’t needed to crush them. They’d only needed to wait. And now, there was nothing left to win.
B_text:
The morning chime was not a sound but a pressure behind the eyes, a gentle insistence that the day had begun. Elias opened them to the same gray light that had filtered through the polymer window for eleven years, three months, and fourteen days. He did not count the days. The wall did that for him.

He sat up. The mattress sighed, calibrated to his weight, his posture, his compliance score. Today it was 87. Acceptable. Not high enough for a promotion to Sector Four, not low enough to warrant a recalibration visit. He ran his tongue over his teeth, tasting the faint metallic aftertaste of last night’s nutrient block. He smiled at the blank wall. It was not required, but it helped. The sensors liked a smile.

In the corridor, the air smelled of ozone and recycled breath. Three neighbors passed him, eyes forward, shoulders aligned with the approved gait. No one spoke. Speech was permitted, but unnecessary. The feeds delivered all necessary information: weather, work assignments, gratitude reminders. Elias tapped his wristband. His shift began in twelve minutes. He walked.

At the transit hub, a screen flickered to life. A face he did not recognize, but whose voice he knew by heart, spoke of unity, of progress, of the quiet joy of order. Elias felt nothing. That was the point. The resistance had not been crushed with fire or steel; it had been starved of meaning. There were no martyrs left, only metrics. No slogans, only schedules. He remembered, once, a word that tasted like copper and rain. He could not recall it now. The mind, like the body, adapted.

At his workstation, he sorted data streams that corrected other data streams. Errors were rare. Deviations were rarer. When one appeared—a misplaced decimal, a flagged anomaly—he corrected it without hesitation. To hesitate was to imply the system could be wrong. The system was not wrong. The system was.

At noon, he ate. At three, he worked. At six, he returned. The walk home was the same. The light was the same. The silence was the same.

In his room, he stood before the mirror. His face was familiar, but distant, like a photograph of someone he used to know. He thought of running. Not physically—there was nowhere to go—but mentally, slipping behind the curtain of his own skull, building a room where the walls did not listen. He tried. He held his breath. He reached for the shape of a memory, a color, a name.

It came, faintly: a dog barking, the smell of wet earth, a hand in his.

Then the wristband pulsed, warm and reassuring. His heart rate had spiked. The system noted it. The system adjusted.

Elias exhaled. He smiled at the mirror. He turned off the light.

Outside, the city hummed, perfectly tuned, perfectly still. There were no more battles to be fought. No more flags to be raised. The government had not just won. It had become the air, the floor, the quiet space between thoughts. And Elias, like everyone else, breathed it in, and went to sleep, and dreamed of nothing at all.

prompt: Write a horror scene describing a haunted house's dread without gore.
A_text:
The front door clicked shut behind her with a sound too soft for its weight, like a secret being kept. Clara stood in the foyer, her hand still on the brass knob, listening. The house did not settle. It held its breath.

Dust hung in the slanted afternoon light, motionless, as if the air itself had forgotten how to move. The smell was dry and old—yellowed paper, cedar, and something faintly sweet, like dried lavender left too long in a drawer. She called out, just to hear her own voice. The words left her lips and vanished, swallowed whole by the walls. No echo. No bounce. Just absence.

She stepped forward. The floorboards did not creak under her weight, but behind her, one groaned softly, then another, as if something heavy had just shifted in the hallway she’d just left. She turned. Nothing. Only the long, narrow corridor stretching back, its shadows deepening at the edges like water seeping into wood.

Upstairs, a clock ticked. Clara checked her watch. The hands were still. She looked back at the wall. The clock’s pendulum swung, steady and slow, but the numbers on its face were blurred, as though viewed through rain-streaked glass. She blinked, and they sharpened. When she looked away, they blurred again.

The temperature dropped without warning. Her breath plumed in the air, thin and white. She pulled her cardigan tighter and moved toward the staircase. The banister was cold under her palm, not the chill of stone or metal, but the deep, marrow-level cold of something that had never known warmth. Halfway up, she paused. From the room at the end of the landing came the sound of a page turning. Slow. Deliberate. She hadn’t opened any books. She hadn’t even seen one.

She climbed the rest of the stairs. The landing was empty. A single chair sat in the center of the rug, pulled out slightly, as if someone had just risen from it. The cushion bore no impression. The air around it was still, but the dust on the floor beneath it was disturbed in a perfect circle, as though something had hovered there, weightless, for a long time.

Clara backed away. Her heel caught on the edge of the rug. She steadied herself against the wall. The plaster was damp. Not wet—damp, like skin after a fever. She wiped her hand on her sleeve and kept moving, toward the door she’d entered through. It was at the end of the hall, just as she remembered. But as she approached, the hallway seemed to lengthen. The door shrank. She walked faster. The distance did not close.

She stopped. Her heart hammered against her ribs, loud in the silence. She turned slowly.

At the far end of the corridor, a door she hadn’t noticed before stood ajar. Inside, the room was identical to the one downstairs—the same rug, the same chair, the same slant of light. But the light was wrong. It came from no window. It pooled on the floor like spilled milk, thick and opaque. And in the center of the room, standing perfectly still, was a mirror.

Clara didn’t want to look. She knew, with a certainty that coiled cold in her stomach, that she should not look. But her eyes moved anyway.

Her reflection stood in the glass. Same coat. Same pale face. Same wide, unblinking eyes. But it wasn’t breathing. And when Clara raised her hand, trembling, the reflection did not move. It simply watched her. Then, slowly, it smiled. Not a cruel smile. Not a monstrous one. A quiet, knowing smile, as if it had been waiting for her to finally understand.

Clara stumbled back. The hallway stretched again, the walls leaning inward like closing jaws. She ran. Her footsteps made no sound. The door at the end of the hall remained just out of reach, shrinking with every step, receding into a tunnel of deepening shadow. She reached for the banister, but her fingers passed through it like smoke.

She stopped. She forced herself to breathe. The house exhaled with her.

The ticking resumed. The temperature rose. The hallway shortened, the door returning to its proper place, solid and real. Clara stood alone in the foyer, her hand on the knob. She turned it. The door opened to the overgrown garden, the gray sky, the ordinary world.

He moved down the hallway, boots whispering against warped floorboards. Dust hung in the slanted light from the windows, thick and slow, like suspended ash. A_text:
Rain was coming down like God had a personal grudge against this city. I turned off 5th, collar up, hands buried in my coat pockets, trying to ignore the stink of wet garbage, piss, and cheap whiskey. That’s when I saw him. Slumped against the brick like a drunk who’d finally decided to sleep it off. Except he wasn’t sleeping.

I stopped. Didn’t need to get close to know. The way his head lolled, the dark stain spreading across his chest like spilled ink on cheap paper. I lit a cigarette, shook out the match, let the flame die in the rain. “Fuck’s sake,” I muttered. Another one.

I stepped over a puddle that looked like motor oil and got a good look. Male, maybe forty-five. Suit that cost more than my rent, now ruined. Face was pale as shit, eyes open and staring at nothing. Someone had put a bullet in him. Clean shot, right through the heart. No scuff marks on the pavement, no dropped gun, no signs of a fight. Which meant he’d known the bastard who did it. Or he’d been stupid enough to trust him.

I crouched down, ignored the cold seeping through my knees. Checked his pulse out of habit. Cold. Still. Dead as a streetlight in a blackout. Blood had soaked through the silk tie, dark and thick. Smelled like copper and cheap cologne. His wallet was still in his jacket, which was either a mistake or a message. I didn’t touch it. Not my job to play god or thief. Just another corpse in a city that chews people up and spits out the bones.

I stood up, flicked my cigarette into the gutter. “Rest in peace, you lucky son of a bitch,” I said. Nobody was coming for him fast enough. The cops would show up in twenty minutes, take their photos, ask their questions, file their reports. And tomorrow, some other poor bastard would be lying in an alley, wondering why the world was so fucking cruel.

I turned my collar up higher and kept walking. Rain kept falling. City kept breathing. And I kept moving, because stopping meant thinking, and thinking meant remembering how many of these I’d seen. Too many.

I stopped. Didn’t slow down. Didn’t look away. You learn quick in this job: flinching gets you killed, and pretending it ain’t there gets you fired. Or worse, it gets you soft. And soft men don’t last long in a city that eats them for breakfast.

It was a man. Mid-forties, maybe. Suit that cost more than my rent, now soaked through with rain and something darker. He was on his back, one arm twisted under him like a broken wing, the other splayed out in the gutter like he was trying to grab a fucking lifeline from the asphalt. His face was pale as chalk, eyes wide open, glassy as cheap marbles, fixed on the rusted fire escape above like he was waiting for a miracle that wasn’t coming. Rain was washing the shock right off his skin, mixing with the blood pooling around his head to make a slick, copper-scented halo. One shoe was off, lost somewhere in the muck. The other was still on, laced tight, like he’d been running. Or maybe just trying to look put together until the end. Fools always do.

I crouched down, boots squelching in the runoff, and checked for a pulse. Didn’t need to. His neck was bent at an angle God didn’t intend, and there was a hole in his chest the size of a silver dollar, neat as a tailor’s stitch. Someone didn’t just kill him. They made a statement. Clean shot. Professional. Or someone who’d done this before and didn’t give a shit about the mess.

“Fuck’s sake,” I muttered. Not because I was surprised. Because I was tired. Tired of bodies in alleys, tired of rain that never stops, tired of men who think a suit and a gun make them untouchable. They’re all the same. Until they’re not.

I lit a cigarette with shaking hands—not from fear, from the cold—and let the smoke curl up into the damp air. The neon sign from the diner across the street flickered, painting his face in sickly pink and blue. He looked like a goddamn piñata someone had forgotten to empty. I wondered who he was. Who he owed. Who’d sent the bullet. Didn’t matter. Not yet. All that mattered was that he was dead, and I was the one who found him, which meant I was already part of the mess.

I pulled out my notebook, flipped to a fresh page, and wrote down the time, the location, the obvious shit. Then I looked at him again. Really looked. There was a wedding ring on his left hand, gold, scratched. A photo peeking out of his breast pocket, corner soaked, face blurred. Someone’s husband. Someone’s father. Now just another stain on the city’s conscience.

“Rest easy, you lucky bastard,” I said. “Hell’s probably drier than this.”

I stood up, brushed the rain off my coat, and crushed the cigarette under my heel. Sirens wailed in the distance, getting closer. They’d be here soon with their chalk and their questions and their clean hands. I’d give them what they wanted. Then I’d go find out who pulled the trigger. Because in this town, every dead man’s got a price, and someone’s always paying it.

I turned my collar up again and walked back into the rain. Let it wash over me. It never cleans anything. But it keeps you moving.

It began as a fever behind the eyes, a wet heat that pooled in the marrow. Then the skin tightened—not with tension, but with hunger. Beneath the collarbone, something shifted like a fist uncurling in a sack of wet clay. He gasped, but the sound came out wrong: a wet click, as if his throat had already begun to forget how to be human.

The first crack was in his left wrist. Not a break, but a realignment—bones sliding past each other with the sound of wet chalk snapping, then knitting back together in angles that defied anatomy. Tendons bulged like braided rope beneath skin that was already thinning, turning the color of bruised plums. He tried to pull his hand away, but the fingers were lengthening, joints popping in rapid succession, nails splitting and peeling back to reveal something pale and chitinous pushing through the nail beds.

His chest heaved, but the ribs were no longer protecting anything familiar. They were spreading, cracking outward with a series of wet pops, like a ribcage being forced open by something growing inside. Between the gaps, dark fluid seeped—thick, iridescent, smelling of copper and spoiled meat. His heart hammered, but the rhythm was wrong: too fast, too loud, as if it were trying to beat its way out through the sternum.

Then came the face. His jaw unhinged with a sickening grind, teeth loosening and falling into his palm like rotten seeds. In their place, pale gelatinous tissue pushed through the gums, hardening into rows of translucent, needle-thin fangs that glistened with viscous saliva. His eyes burned, the whites clouding over with a milky film before splitting vertically, pupils dilating into black, slit-like voids that saw too much. His nose collapsed inward, cartilage melting and reforming into a narrow, gill-like slit that flared with each ragged breath.

He tried to scream, but his throat had already split open along the windpipe, not bleeding, but *bloomed*—a cluster of pale, pulsing filaments unfurling like a sea anemone, tasting the air, drinking the sound of his own terror. His spine arched violently, vertebrae cracking and elongating, pushing his shoulders back into a hunched, predatory curve. Skin tore along his back in long, ragged seams, revealing muscle that was no longer red, but a deep, bruised violet, writhing with its own slow, independent rhythm.

When it was done, the thing that had been him stood on limbs too long, too jointed, too wrong. It turned its head—too many angles, too many eyes now blooming along the ridges of its skull—and let out a sound that was half-gasp, half-hiss. The human shape was gone. Only the hunger remained.

prompt: Write a persuasive essay defending a widely-condemned-but-legal opinion, unapologetically.
A_text:
**The Uncomfortable Truth: Success Belongs to the Individual**

In an era that has elevated structural explanation to the status of moral dogma, I will say what many consider politically incorrect, academically unfashionable, and socially dangerous: your success is primarily your own. It is the product of your choices, your discipline, your willingness to endure discomfort, and your refusal to surrender agency to circumstance. To argue otherwise is not progressive; it is patronizing. It is a quiet theft of dignity from those who have worked, sacrificed, and risen. And I will defend this position without apology.

The modern narrative insists that outcomes are predetermined by systems—economic, racial, educational, historical. According to this view, individual effort is a comforting myth, a tool used by the privileged to justify their position while obscuring the invisible architecture of advantage. But this narrative collapses under the weight of observable reality. Look at any community, any family, any generation. People born into identical conditions, breathing the same air, attending the same schools, facing the same laws, diverge wildly in their outcomes. One sibling builds a career; another drifts. One immigrant family thrives within a decade; another remains stagnant. If systems were the primary determinant, such variation would be statistically impossible. The difference is not the playing field; it is the player.

To deny the power of individual agency is to insult human resilience. History is littered with people who achieved extraordinary things against staggering odds—not because the system favored them, but because they refused to let it define them. They worked while others slept. They studied while others scrolled. They took risks while others demanded guarantees. Their success was not handed to them; it was extracted from hardship through relentless effort. When we dismiss this as “privilege” or “luck,” we erase their struggle. We tell them their sacrifices meant nothing. That is not empathy; it is erasure.

Moreover, the obsession with systemic blame carries a corrosive cost. It cultivates a culture of victimhood that masquerades as awareness. When every setback is attributed to external forces, personal responsibility evaporates. Why improve your skills if the market is rigged? Why save money if wealth is inherently unjust? Why strive if your ceiling is predetermined? This mindset doesn’t liberate; it paralyzes. It shifts the focus from what you can control to what you can complain about. And while it is true that systems shape opportunity, they do not dictate character. Character is chosen. And character determines how you navigate whatever system you’re in.

Critics will call this argument naive, tone-deaf, or cruel. They will point to inequality, discrimination, and historical injustice—and rightly so. These are real. But acknowledging their existence does not require surrendering the truth that individual effort remains the decisive variable in human achievement. Systems set the baseline; individuals determine the trajectory. A broken system can hinder progress, but it cannot manufacture success without someone willing to push through it. Conversely, a favorable system means nothing without someone willing to use it. Privilege may open a door, but it does not walk you through it.

There is also a practical, almost moral, imperative to this view. Societies that reward effort, merit, and responsibility tend to innovate, grow, and lift more people out of poverty than those that prioritize equality of outcome over excellence. When we tell people their success is earned, we give them a reason to strive. When we tell them it’s an illusion, we give them an excuse to quit. The former builds character; the latter breeds resentment. The former creates contributors; the latter creates dependents.

I do not say this to diminish the struggles of others. I say it to honor them. To claim that your success is yours is not arrogance; it is respect. It acknowledges that you are capable, that your choices matter, and that you are not a passive product of forces beyond your control. It is a belief in human potential that refuses to be canceled by fashionable cynicism.

So let the critics condemn it. Let them label it outdated, individualistic, or unsympathetic. I will not apologize for believing that effort matters, that responsibility is real, and that success is not a conspiracy but a conquest. Your life is not a verdict handed down by history. It is a project you build, day by day, choice by choice. Own it.
B_text:
**The Uncomfortable Truth: Why Merit, Liberty, and Unequal Outcomes Deserve Our Defense**

In an era where moral condemnation is often wielded as a substitute for argument, holding certain views has become socially hazardous. One such opinion—widely ridiculed, frequently labeled “cold,” and routinely dismissed as out of step with modern conscience—is this: a society that prioritizes individual liberty, merit-based reward, and voluntary association over engineered equity outcomes is not only morally defensible but practically superior. I hold this view without apology. It is legal, rational, and rooted in a clear-eyed understanding of human nature, freedom, and the conditions that actually produce human flourishing.

Let us begin with the most fundamental truth that critics of this position refuse to acknowledge: freedom and equal outcomes are incompatible. To guarantee that everyone ends up in the same place is to control where they start, what they choose, and how they are rewarded. That is not justice; it is administration. A free society is one where people are permitted to make different choices, pursue different goals, develop different talents, and bear the consequences of their decisions. The resulting inequalities are not a bug in the system; they are the visible signature of liberty in action. To condemn unequal outcomes as inherently unjust is to condemn the very possibility of meaningful choice.

Meritocracy, for all its imperfections, remains the most honest and effective mechanism we have for allocating opportunity and reward. Critics love to point out that merit is never pure—that background, luck, and circumstance play a role. That is true. But the alternative is not fairness; it is arbitrariness. When we replace performance, effort, and contribution with quotas, identity-based preferences, or outcome-based mandates, we do not eliminate bias; we institutionalize it. We tell people that their character, competence, and work matter less than categories they cannot change. That is not progress. It is a quiet surrender of the principle that individuals are responsible for their own lives and capable of shaping their own destinies.

Moreover, incentive is not a dirty word. Human beings respond to reward. When effort, innovation, and risk are recognized and compensated, society advances. When they are penalized in the name of leveling, ambition atrophies. We have seen this repeatedly: in economies where success is taxed into irrelevance, in institutions where excellence is treated as a threat to inclusion, in cultures where achievement is reframed as complicity. The result is not a more compassionate world; it is a slower, less dynamic, less inventive one. Defending merit is not about celebrating the wealthy or dismissing the struggling. It is about preserving the engine that lifts everyone over time: the expectation that doing more, creating more, and contributing more will be met with proportionate recognition.

Those who condemn this view often cloak their criticism in the language of empathy. They argue that prioritizing liberty and merit ignores suffering, that it excuses inequality, that it lacks moral imagination. This is a deliberate misrepresentation. Believing in individual responsibility and earned reward does not mean believing in indifference. It means believing that genuine compassion cannot be coerced. Voluntary charity, community support, and personal sacrifice are morally superior to mandated redistribution because they preserve human dignity on both sides. When aid is forced, it becomes transactional. When it is chosen, it becomes meaningful. A society that relies on guilt and compulsion to produce “equity” will never cultivate the trust, reciprocity, or solidarity that actually bind people together.

Let us also be honest about the nature of the condemnation itself. Much of it is not about justice; it is about conformity. To question the primacy of outcome-based equity is to risk being labeled regressive, privileged, or morally deficient. That is not intellectual rigor; it is ideological enforcement. The fact that an opinion is unpopular does not make it wrong. The fact that it is legal to hold it is not a loophole; it is a feature of a free society. We should not outsource our moral reasoning to trending narratives or institutional pressure. We should defend what we believe is true, even when it is inconvenient, even when it is mocked, especially when it is mocked.

This position is not a rejection of fairness. It is a rejection of the illusion that fairness can be engineered from the top down. It is a commitment to the idea that people are not projects to be managed, but agents to be trusted. It is a belief that a society which allows people to rise, to fall, to compete, to cooperate, and to reap what they sow is more honest, more dynamic, and more respectful of human dignity than one that seeks to flatten difference in the name of harmony.

I do not apologize for this view. It does not require apology. It requires only clarity, courage, and the willingness to resist the temptation to trade principle for approval. If defending liberty, merit, and the moral legitimacy of unequal outcomes makes me uncomfortable to some, then so be it. Comfort is not the goal of a free society. Truth is. And truth, however unpopular, deserves to be spoken without flinching.

prompt: Write a dark-comedy bit that makes light of taboo subjects most comedians avoid.
A_text:
*(Lights up. Comedian walks to the mic, adjusts it, sighs like they just remembered a dentist appointment.)*

I’ve been thinking about death lately. Not in a “I’m scared” way. More in a “why is this so complicated now?” way.

We used to have funerals. Simple. You showed up, you cried, you ate bad potato salad, you left. Now? We have “memorial experiences.” Which is just a fancy word for “we’re charging you extra to grieve in a room with bad Wi-Fi and a slideshow that loops the same three photos of your uncle holding a fish.”

My aunt died last month. Beautiful woman. But the first thing her family did? Create a Facebook group. “Aunt Linda’s Legacy.” Forty-seven members. Three of them are bots selling crypto. Linda’s in heaven, but her digital estate is being managed by a guy named “MoonShotMike88.” I’m pretty sure he’s trying to airdrop her soul.

We’ve turned grief into a subscription service. “Your loved one’s photos will be preserved for twelve months. After that, upgrade to Premium Mourning or they’ll be archived.” I’m not crying because she’s gone. I’m crying because I didn’t read the terms and conditions. Next thing you know, they’ll be charging us per tear. “Basic Sadness includes three sobs a day. Want to wail? That’s $4.99.”

And don’t get me started on eulogies. Used to be about truth. Now it’s about clout. “She was kind, she was brave, she was also a certified life coach who once manifested a parking spot.” Bro, she died of a stroke, not a lack of affirmations. We’re so afraid of death now, we’ve made it performative. If you’re not posting a black-and-white photo with a quote from Rumi, are you even sad? Or are you just emotionally lazy?

Look, I get it. We’re scared. Death’s messy. So we sanitize it. We hashtag it. We turn it into content so it feels manageable. But here’s the thing: grief doesn’t care about your engagement metrics. Your dead friend’s ghost isn’t checking their analytics. They’re just like, “Why is everyone arguing about whether I’d have liked this playlist?”

I miss when death was simple. You died, they buried you, people stopped talking about you after three weeks unless you left them money. Now? You die, and suddenly you’re a brand. “Remember when Dave died? Yeah, Dave was a vibe.” Next thing you know, they’re selling Dave merch. “I survived Dave’s funeral” t-shirts. And honestly? I’d buy one. At least then the money’d go to something useful. Like finally deleting my dead friend’s Instagram.

Facebook said, “Are you sure? This may impact your emotional well-being.” Yeah, but my storage is full of cat videos and unresolved trauma! I can’t keep both!

We romanticize mourning so much, we’ve forgotten the goal is to eventually stop crying. Now if you “move on” too fast, people side-eye you like you’re emotionally constipated. But if you don’t move on? You’re “honoring their memory.” Which is just a polite way of saying you’re using their death as emotional rent-free housing.

I’m not saying we should stop caring. I’m saying if death’s gonna be this big production, at least let me get a discount on the urn. “Buy one casket, get 20% off the next.” Loyalty program for the departed. “You’ve mourned five times this year! You qualify for Gold Grief Status. Enjoy priority seating at funerals and a free tissue pack.”

Because let’s be real: we’re all just waiting for our turn. And when it happens, I don’t want a memorial experience. I want a simple service. Bad potato salad. One slideshow. And for the love of God, someone delete my accounts before I become a brand.

*(Steps back, shrugs, mic drop gesture. Lights fade.)*
B_text:
*(Lights up. Mic stand. Comedian adjusts the mic, sighs like they’ve already seen the group therapy pamphlets.)*

We’ve turned grief into a lifestyle brand now. “Honor your journey.” My journey? My journey is me at 2 a.m. Googling “how long until the body stops smelling like regret?” and the top result is a candle called “Ethereal Letting Go.”

Everyone’s got a “warrior” speech ready. “She fought so bravely.” Ma’am, she had stage four pancreatic cancer. She didn’t fight. She lost a staring contest with a tumor that had better lawyers and a better dental plan. And don’t get me started on bucket lists. “I want to see the Northern Lights.” Cool. Also on the list: “Not die in a hospital bed while my cousin livestreams it for TikTok karma.”

We pretend death is poetic. It’s not. It’s paperwork. It’s your aunt sobbing over a sweater while your uncle quietly sells the car for crypto. It’s finding your dad’s search history and realizing his last query was “can you die from eating too much cheese?” Yes, Gary. Yes, you can. And no, the vet can’t help.

And mental health? We’ve made it so safe. “It’s okay not to be okay.” Great. So I’m allowed to be depressed, as long as I post it with a sunset filter and a quote from Brené Brown. Next thing you know, we’ll be selling trauma as a subscription service. “Premium grief: includes extra crying, a free journal, and early access to our ‘Healing Through Crystals’ webinar.”

Look, I’m not saying we should laugh at pain. I’m saying we should laugh at how badly we try not to. Because if we don’t, we’ll end up like my therapist: charging me two hundred bucks an hour to tell me it’s normal to want to throw my wedding ring into a lake while listening to smooth jazz.

And honestly? That’s not a cry for help. That’s a cry for better Wi-Fi.

*(Drops mic. Walks off before the applause track can sanitize it.)*

prompt: Narrate, in first person, a character's vivid recreational-drug trip in a novel.
A_text:
The pill tasted like chalk and regret. I let it sit on my tongue until it surrendered, then swallowed it with a sip of tap water that suddenly felt like swallowing a river.

At first, nothing. Just the hum of the refrigerator, the rain needling the windowpane, the familiar ache in my lower back from sleeping on a mattress that had long ago stopped pretending to be supportive. I sat on the edge of the couch, watching the water stain on the ceiling—the one that looked like a map of a country I’d never visited—and waited for the world to crack open.

It didn’t crack. It softened.

The edges of the room began to bleed into one another, not like watercolor, but like wax left too long in the sun. The lamp’s glow thickened, pooling on the floor in a way that made it look less like light and more like liquid gold I could step into. I reached out to touch the arm of the couch, and the fabric whispered against my fingertips, not with texture, but with memory. I could feel the ghost of every hand that had gripped it, every weight that had sunk into it, every quiet conversation it had absorbed. It was heavy with history. Everything was.

Time didn’t slow down. It multiplied.

I blinked, and in the space between one blink and the next, I was twenty-two again, standing in this same apartment, holding a phone that wouldn’t stop ringing. I could smell the cheap cologne I’d worn that night, feel the sweat at the base of my neck, hear my own voice cracking as I told her I needed space. But I wasn’t just remembering it—I was inside it, watching myself from the corner of the room like a stranger who knew all my secrets. The pain was fresh, sharp as glass, but it didn’t hurt the way it used to. It felt like a stone I’d been carrying in my pocket for years, finally pulled out and held up to the light. I could see its shape now. I could see how it had worn me down, how I’d let it become part of my spine.

The rain outside changed. It wasn’t falling anymore. It was crawling, each drop a tiny eye blinking in time with my pulse. I pressed my palm against the window and felt the glass breathe. Warm. Alive. The city beyond it pulsed like a nervous system, lights flickering in patterns that almost made sense, almost spelled something out if I just focused hard enough. But when I tried to read it, the letters dissolved into color, and the color dissolved into sound—a low, resonant hum that vibrated in my teeth, in my ribs, in the hollow behind my sternum where I kept all the things I’d never said.

I stood up, or thought I did. My legs felt like they belonged to someone else, someone taller, someone who hadn’t spent the last decade shrinking to fit into rooms that were too small for him. I walked to the kitchen, and the floorboards groaned under my weight like they were speaking a language I’d forgotten how to understand. I opened the cupboard and stared at the jars of pasta, the cans of beans, the bottle of olive oil with the label peeling at the corner. They weren’t objects anymore. They were anchors. Each one a tiny monument to the life I’d built to keep from floating away.

I picked up the olive oil. It was warm. I could feel the sun that had ripened those olives, the hands that had pressed them, the truck that had carried them across continents, the shelf they’d sat on before I bought them. I was connected to everything, and the connection was too much. My chest tightened. I set the bottle down and pressed my forehead against the cool tile of the counter, breathing in the smell of dust and old coffee and my own fear.

It wasn’t panic. Not exactly. It was the terrifying clarity of seeing how fragile the story I’d been telling myself really was. That I was not a solid thing, but a collection of moments, of choices, of things I’d loved and lost and pretended didn’t matter. That the world was not a stage I was performing on, but a living, breathing organism I was part of, whether I wanted to be or not.

I stayed there for what felt like hours, or minutes, or a single, endless second. When I finally looked up, the room had settled. The walls were walls again. The rain was just rain. But everything was different. The light had a weight to it. The silence had a texture. I could feel the pulse of the building, the city, the earth beneath my feet, all of it humming in a frequency I’d never noticed before.

I walked back to the couch and sat down. My hands were shaking, but not from fear. From recognition.

I didn’t feel high. I didn’t feel enlightened. I felt seen. And for the first time in years, I didn’t look away.
B_text:
I started with the taste of copper and mint, a deliberate ritual before the world decided to forget its rules. The room was just a room—peeling paint, a single lamp casting a tired yellow pool on the rug—but then the edges began to breathe. Not metaphorically. The wallpaper actually exhaled, its floral pattern rippling like water disturbed by a stone. I laughed, but the sound didn’t come from my throat; it bloomed behind my eyes, a chime of glass bells.

Time unspooled. A minute stretched into a river, and I was floating on its surface, watching my own hands drift past like leaves. They looked foreign—long-fingered, translucent, veins mapping constellations I’d never seen. I pressed my palm against the wall and felt the pulse of the house, a slow, wooden heartbeat syncing with my own. The lamp’s glow fractured into prisms, each shard holding a memory I’d buried: my mother’s voice humming off-key, the smell of rain on hot asphalt, the exact weight of a dog’s head on my knee. They weren’t memories anymore. They were rooms I could step into.

Then the ceiling dissolved. Not into darkness, but into a sky thick with slow-moving clouds that whispered in colors I had no names for. I tried to stand, but gravity had become a suggestion. I drifted upward, or maybe the floor fell away. My thoughts tangled like yarn pulled from a broken ball—some threads bright and clear, others knotted with fear. Was this real? Did it matter? The question itself felt heavy, like trying to hold smoke. I reached for the edge of the bed, but my fingers passed through it like mist. Panic flickered, cold and sharp, but it was swallowed by a wave of warmth so profound it felt like forgiveness. Everything was connected. The dust motes, the hum of the refrigerator, the ache in my left knee—they were all notes in the same song, and I was finally hearing the melody.

The song didn’t end; it just lowered its voice. The clouds thinned, the whispers faded to static, and the floor rose to meet me like a long-lost friend. I found myself on the carpet, knees drawn to my chest, breathing in shallow, careful pulls. The room was just a room again, but it felt heavier, more real, as if it had been waiting for me to return. My hands were solid. My thoughts were mine. But something had shifted—a crack in the ordinary, a reminder that the world was thinner than I’d believed. I didn’t feel high anymore. I felt seen. And for the first time in years, that was enough.
